title: Get the code
heading: Clone the repo
text: Hyperion pulls in a few libraries as Git submodules (Jolt, zlib, xatlas, meshoptimizer, ...), so clone with --recursive: git clone --recursive https://github.com/HyperionGameTech/HyperionEngine.git You'll land on the dev branch, which is where all the day-to-day work happens.

title: Get the code

text: Run this from the repo root: git submodule update --init --recursive

title: Build the engine
heading: What you'll need
text: On every platform: CMake 3.27 or newer. .NET SDK, with dotnet on your PATH. The editor UI is built with Avalonia on .NET 10, so the editor needs it. Per platform: Platform You'll also need Windows Visual Studio 2026 (MSVC, or the Clang that ships with it), and vcpkg with the VCPKG_ROOT environment variable pointing at it. macOS The Vulkan SDK, plus brew install molten-vk (or run Tools/Scripts/InstallDependenciesMac.sh). MoltenVK translates Vulkan to Metal for us. Linux GCC or Clang, the Vulkan SDK with VULKAN_SDK set, and the X11, OpenAL and Vulkan loader dev packages. On Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install libx11-dev libopenal-dev libvulkan-dev. Ninja is optional. Android The Android NDK (we test with NDK 29), and Ninja on your PATH. See Android. Web emsdk with the EMSDK environment variable pointing at it, and Ninja on your PATH.

title: Build the engine
heading: Build it
text: From the root of the repo:

title: Build the engine
heading: Windows
text: build.bat Release To build with Clang instead of MSVC: build.bat Release Clang On Windows the default rendering backend is DirectX 12. To build with Vulkan instead, add Vulkan (build.bat Release Vulkan); that needs the Vulkan SDK installed, with VULKAN_SDK set.

title: Build the engine
heading: macOS
text: ./build.sh Release To generate an Xcode project: ./build.sh Xcode Release

title: Build the engine
heading: Linux
text: ./build.sh Release CMake uses your system's default compiler, usually GCC. To use Clang, set CC=clang CXX=clang++ first. Add ninja (./build.sh Release ninja) to build with Ninja instead of Makefiles. The script asks if you want to regenerate the CMake project first, and moves on without it after 3 seconds. Answer yes if you've added or removed source files. Pass Regenerate to always regenerate, or NoWait to skip the question. Use Release (or RelWithDebInfo) on Windows. Debug builds work, but run very slowly.

title: Build the engine
heading: Other options
text: Argument What it does Shipping An optimized build without the editor, tests or commandlets. See packaging. Runtime The engine without the editor (.NET stays on, for C# games). Goes to Binaries/<Platform>-Runtime/. Android Builds for Android. Web Builds for the browser (WebAssembly and WebGPU). ARM64 Builds for Windows on ARM. Needs the C++ Clang tools for Windows Visual Studio component. Ninja Uses Ninja and clang-cl instead of a Visual Studio solution.

title: Build the engine
heading: CodeGen
text: CodeGen is a build tool that reads the engine's headers and generates the reflection, serialization and scripting bindings. It runs automatically when CMake configures, so you don't normally run it yourself. Its output goes into Source/Generated/. Don't edit those files by hand; they're overwritten on every run.

title: Build the engine
heading: Run it
text: Build output goes to Binaries/<Platform>/<Config>/, for example Binaries/Windows/Release/, Binaries/Mac/Release/ or Binaries/Linux/Release/. The main executables are: Hyperion.Editor (.exe on Windows), the editor. hyperion-sample (.exe on Windows), the C++ sample game. CSharpGame (.exe on Windows), the C# sample game. Commandlets like PrecompileShaders land in the same folder. See Console & CVars.

title: Build the engine
heading: Troubleshooting
text: "VCPKG_ROOT not set": Windows builds need it. Point it at your vcpkg install, then open a new terminal. CMake fails with CodeGen errors: run Tools/Scripts/BuildCodeGen.bat (or .sh) on its own to see what actually went wrong. Metal API validation errors on macOS: the generated Xcode project turns Metal API Validation off for you. If you've made your own scheme, turn it off under the Options tab. Rendering goes through MoltenVK, which the validator reports false errors for. The full Compiling the Engine guide in the repo covers Android, optional dependencies and IDE setup.

title: Glossary
heading: Core types
text: Object Anything built on Hyperion's object system. It gets reflection, ref counting, serialization and a unique ID. Those IDs only last for the current run, so don't save them anywhere. Class Runtime info about a type: its name, fields, methods and parents. Mark a class with HYP_CLASS() and CodeGen takes care of the rest. Handle A strong reference to an object. When the last handle goes away, so does the object. Make one with MakeHandle<T>(). WeakHandle is the non-owning version.

title: Glossary
heading: Scenes and what's in them
text: World The top of the tree. It holds your scenes, plus world-wide things like physics and audio. Scene A level, or a region of your world. It's a tree of nodes, with an octree on the side for fast spatial queries. Node Something with a position, rotation and scale that can have children. Children move with their parent. Entity A node you can attach components to. Most things in your game will be entities. Component A chunk of data attached to an entity, like a mesh or a transform. Components describe what an entity is. System Code that runs over every entity with a certain set of components, in parallel. Components are the data; systems are the logic. Subsystem World-wide logic that isn't tied to entities or components, like a day/night clock. It gets an Update() call every frame. Camera, Light Entities that view the scene and light it. View What a camera sees: the slice of your scene that gets rendered. You can have a few at once, like one for the main camera and one for shadows. Swatch A saved look for your world, like Noon or Dusk. Each swatch can have its own baked lighting.

title: Glossary
heading: Rendering
text: Render proxy Rendering runs on its own thread. Scene objects hand their data over through render proxies: the game thread writes, the render thread reads. Render group Objects that render the same way, batched together for instancing and culling. Think of it as roughly one graphics pipeline.

title: A tour of the editor
text: The editor's panels, toolbar, viewport controls and shortcuts.

title: A tour of the editor
heading: The panels
text: Panel What it's for Scene Everything in your scene, as a tree. The dropdown at the top switches between scenes, or adds a new one. Inspector All about whatever you've got selected: its components, tags, layers, script and properties. Viewport The 3D view, in the middle of the window. Assets Your project's content, in folders. Search it, Import... things, or make something with Add.... See projects. Console Logs, plus a spot to type commands. See Console & CVars. Asset editors open as panels on the right. To restore the default layout, use Layout › Reset Layout in the gear menu.

title: A tour of the editor
heading: The toolbar
text: There's no menu bar. Everything lives in the toolbar, roughly left to right: New Project, Open (its arrow lists recent projects) and Save. Undo, redo, copy and paste. Select All, with Select All in Viewport and Select None under its arrow. Layers, and the active swatch. Bake, for baking lighting. Add, for putting new things in your scene: lights, probes, volumes and more. Translate, Rotate and Scale, to pick what the gizmo does, plus grid snapping. The arrow next to snapping has the grid settings: snap size, rotation snap and offset. Mesh tools, terrain tools (sculpting and painting) and paint tools (decals, instances and ground cover). Build, for building and packaging your game. Play, Pause and Stop. More in play-in-editor. The gear menu, with World Settings, LOD, Ghost Mode, Show Stats and Layout.

title: A tour of the editor
heading: Viewports
text: The gear menu's Layout picks how many viewports you get: Layout Views Single Viewport One perspective view. This is the default. Four Viewports Top and Front above, Side and Perspective below. Perspective + Three A large perspective view, over a row of Top, Front and Side. In the Top, Front and Side views, drag with any mouse button to pan, and scroll to zoom.

Camera speed and mouse sensitivity are set with the Editor.Camera.MovementSpeed and Editor.Camera.MouseSensitivity CVars.

title: Working with projects
text: A project holds your game's scenes, assets, scripts and settings in one folder.

title: Working with projects
heading: The start screen
text: The editor opens on a start screen: New Project makes a project from the blank template. Browse... opens an existing .hypproject file. Recent Projects lists what you've opened before. Use the arrow keys and Enter to pick one. Right-click one to pin it, show it in Explorer, or remove it from the list. Tick Open last project on startup to skip the start screen next time. To turn that back off, untick Always Open Most Recent Project on Startup under the arrow next to Open in the toolbar.

title: Working with projects
heading: New projects
text: New Project (on the start screen, or in the toolbar) asks where to save the project first, and creates a folder for it named after the project. It starts with a main scene, a sun, the ground, and a player with a camera.

title: Working with projects
heading: Opening a project
text: Use Open in the toolbar and pick a .hypproject file, or pick one from the recent projects under its arrow.

title: Working with projects
heading: What's inside
text: Projects/MyGame/ MyGame.hypproject AssetFolders.txt Content/ Materials/ Meshes/ Prefabs/ Scenes/ Scripts/ Textures/ Worlds/ Saved/ The .hypproject file is the project itself, and Content holds your assets, sorted into folders by type. Assets are saved as .hmf files, a readable text format, with larger binary data in .blob files next to them. Saved holds editor state, like the thumbnail on the start screen. A project with C++ or C# code also has Source, Build and Binaries folders, and packaging adds Packaged. See Building your game. Projects made before the Content folder keep their assets next to the .hypproject file, and still work as they are.

title: Working with projects
heading: The Assets panel
text: The Assets panel has its own folders, separate from how files are laid out on disk. Make as many as you like and organize assets however you want: Add... › Folder, or right-click a folder, to make one. Right-click to rename or delete it. Drag assets and folders onto a folder, or onto the path at the top, to move them. Moves can be undone. Import... and Add... put new assets in the folder you're in. The search box searches the current folder, or everything from the top. Filter by type, and sort by name, date modified or type. Key Action Enter Open Backspace Up a folder F2 Rename a folder Delete Delete These folders are saved in AssetFolders.txt, and only the editor uses them.

title: Working with projects
heading: Saving
text: There's no separate "save scene". Saving the project saves everything that's changed, scenes included. The editor camera position is saved with the project too. Close with unsaved changes, and the editor will ask whether to save, discard, or cancel.

title: Prefabs
text: A prefab is a reusable group of nodes that you can place in any scene.

title: Prefabs
heading: Making a prefab
text: In the Scene panel, right-click a node and pick Save as Prefab... Select a few nodes first to bundle them together. Give it a name (no spaces) and hit Create. The node you started with becomes an instance of your new prefab. It's marked with in the Scene panel. To create an empty prefab: Assets › Add... › Prefab.

title: Prefabs
heading: Placing it
text: Drag the prefab from Assets into the viewport, or right-click it and pick Add to Current Scene.

title: Prefabs
heading: Making changes
text: Tweak an instance, then right-click it and choose Sync Prefab to update the prefab itself. To add nodes to an existing prefab, select them, right-click, and pick the prefab under Add to Prefab. To edit a prefab on its own, right-click an instance and choose Edit Prefab. The prefab opens in place of your scene; when you're done, pick Exit Prefab Edit from the dropdown at the top of the Scene panel. All of these actions can be undone.

title: Play-in-editor
text: Run your game inside the editor, without making a separate build.

title: Play-in-editor
heading: Play, pause, stop
text: The Play, Pause and Stop buttons are near the right end of the toolbar. Play saves your project first, and Stop restores that saved state, so changes made while playing are discarded. A project that's never been saved asks you to save it before playing. Ghost Mode (in the gear menu) gives you a free camera while playing. Move it with W A S D, Space and Ctrl.

title: Play-in-editor
heading: Network modes
text: Pick a mode from the arrow next to Play. The option you select will be saved as the default play mode for next time. Mode Play button action Play Local The game runs in the editor in single player Play as Client The editor connects to the server at Host:Port. Start the server first, separately; see Running a server. Play as Dedicated Server The editor hosts the game on Port. It has no player of its own; players spawn for clients that connect. Stop disconnects or stops hosting. The same menu has Play in Web Browser, which builds the game for the web and opens it in your browser. See Web. Nothing is replicated unless the game's world has the IsReplicated flag. It's part of the world's default flags, so a world saved with Flags = Default has it. But it is something to look into if you're having issues in this area. On your filesystem, open your project's Content/Worlds/MainWorld.hmf file and look at its Flags.

title: Play-in-editor
heading: Network Settings
text: Open Network Settings... from the same menu. Setting Default Used for Host 127.0.0.1 The server Play as Client connects to Port 9192 The game server port, in both networked modes Cache Server Port 8081 In Play as Dedicated Server, serves your saved project to clients that connect

title: Play-in-editor
heading: More players
text: When the editor plays as a dedicated server, run the game against it to add players, syncing content from the editor's cache server: hyperion-sample --host=127.0.0.1 --gameport=9192 --cacheserver=http://127.0.0.1:8081

title: Building your game (C++)
text: Give your project its own C++ code, and build it into a game you can run outside the editor.

title: Building your game (C++)
heading: The Build menu
text: Build, near the right end of the toolbar, has everything on this page. Item What it does Generate Game Project... Adds a C# or C++ project to your project folder. Once it exists, this becomes Open C# Project Folder or Open C++ Project Folder. Change Language... Switches the project between C# and C++. Only applicable when source files haven't been changed. Build Game Compiles that project into a game executable. Reload Game Loads the latest build of your C++ game into the editor. See In the editor. Package Game Makes a standalone copy of the game to share. See Packaging a build. Package for Web Builds the game for the browser. See Web. Packaging Settings... Settings for packaged builds - see Packaging settings. This page covers C++; switch to C# at the top of the page. This page uses Windows paths. On Linux and macOS, the build needs CMake and the same C++ compiler the engine was built with (g++ or clang++) on your PATH, and uses Ninja if it's installed. Output goes to Binaries/Linux/ or Binaries/Mac/, executables have no .exe, and the build script is build.sh.

title: Building your game (C++)
heading: Generate the C++ project
text: Save your project first, then choose Build › Generate Game Project... and pick C++. The editor adds a Source folder to your project and opens it (or opens it in Visual Studio, if Open in Visual Studio is ticked): Projects/MyGame/ MyGame.hypproject Source/ CMakeLists.txt Game/ MyGameGame.hpp MyGameGame.cpp Launcher/ main.cpp The names come from your .hypproject file's name. These files are yours to edit, and the editor won't overwrite them. File What's in it Game/MyGameGame.hpp, .cpp Your Game class. This is where your game's code goes. Launcher/main.cpp The executable's entry point. It starts the engine and creates your Game. CMakeLists.txt Builds the two above against the engine. Every .cpp and .hpp under Game/ is picked up automatically.

title: Building your game (C++)
heading: Your Game class
text: The generated class overrides a few hooks from Game: void MyGameGame::OnLaunch() { Game::OnLaunch(); HYP_LOG(Game, Info, "MyGameGame launched"); } void MyGameGame::OnUpdate(float delta) { Game::OnUpdate(delta); } Function When it's called OnLaunch Once, after the startup world has loaded. OnUpdate Every frame, with the time since the last frame. OnInputEvent For each input event. Returns true if something handled it. BeforeConnectingToServer When the game starts as a client, before it has joined a server. BeforeContentLoaded, AfterContentLoaded Either side of loading the startup world. The last three drive a plain status screen (ShowStatus and HideStatus in the same file), so the window says "Loading...", "Connecting to..." or why it couldn't connect instead of sitting black. Swap it for your own loading and connect screens. CodeGenTool doesn't run on game code yet, so HYP_CLASS() and friends aren't available here. The generated .cpp registers the class by hand; leave that block at the bottom of the file in place.

title: Building your game (C++)
heading: Build
text: Choose Build › Build Game. Compiler output goes to the Console, and you'll get a message box if the build fails. The build needs Visual Studio, or the Visual Studio Build Tools, with: The Desktop development with C++ workload. C++ Clang tools for Windows. Not needed if you built the editor yourself with MSVC. C++ CMake tools for Windows. If something's missing, the editor tells you what and offers to install the Build Tools for you. The result lands in your project's Binaries folder: Projects/MyGame/ Binaries/Windows/ MyGame.exe MyGameGame.dll hyperion.dll Config/ Build/Windows/ Build.bat MyGameGame.dll holds your game's code, and MyGame.exe is the launcher that loads it. The engine's own libraries and config are copied in next to them. Build.bat runs the same build outside the editor.

title: Building your game (C++)
heading: Run it
text: Run MyGame.exe. It loads your project's content straight from the project folder, so there's nothing to cook: save in the editor, and the next run has your changes. By default the game starts in single player. The same executable also hosts and joins multiplayer games: Command What it does MyGame Single player MyGame --server A headless dedicated server MyGame --singleplayer=false --host=127.0.0.1 Joins the server at that address The single player default comes from Binaries/Windows/Config/GlobalConfig.json; anything you pass on the command line overrides it. More in Running a server.

title: Building your game (C++)
heading: In the editor
text: Once the game is built, the editor loads MyGameGame.dll when it opens your project, and play-in-editor runs your Game class.

title: Building your game (C++)
heading: Hot reload
text: You can rebuild while the project is open. When MyGameGame.dll changes, the editor loads the new build by itself, whether you built from the editor, Visual Studio or Build.bat. To force a reload, use Build › Reload Game. Either way, it waits until you stop playing, and Play always runs the newest build. To turn the automatic reload off, set the Editor.AutoReloadGameModule CVar to false.

title: Building your game (C#)
text: Write your game's code in C#, with a Visual Studio solution the editor generates for you.

title: Building your game (C#)
heading: Generate the project
text: Save your project first, then choose Build › Generate Game Project... A project's sources can be written in either C# or C++. This page covers C#; switch to C++ at the top of the page. To switch after selection, use Build › Change Language.... You can only change this when there are no changed files after generating the project. Generate adds these to your project folder: Projects/MyGame/ MyGame.hypproject MyGame.slnx Source/ MyGame.csproj MyGameGame.cs Program.cs Hyperion.Local.props

title: Building your game (C#)
heading: Your Game class
text: The generated class overrides three hooks from Game: Method When it's called OnLaunch Once, after the startup world has loaded. OnUpdate Every frame, with the time since the last frame. OnShutdown When the game shuts down, before the world is torn down. The editor finds your class by name. Keep it named after your project with Game on the end (MyGameGame for MyGame.hypproject).

title: Building your game (C#)
heading: Build
text: Build from either place: In Visual Studio, Build › Build Solution (Ctrl+Shift+B). In the editor, Build › Build Game. Compiler output goes to the Console. Both need the .NET 10 SDK. The result lands in your project's Binaries folder, next to a copy of the engine: Projects/MyGame/ Binaries/Windows/ MyGame.exe MyGame.dll hyperion.dll Config/ MyGame.exe runs the game on its own, loading content straight from the project folder. It takes the same command line as a C++ game; see Run it.

title: Building your game (C#)
heading: Play it in the editor
text: Press Play. The editor loads MyGame.dll and runs your Game class in play-in-editor.

title: Building your game (C#)
heading: Package
text: Build › Package Game works the same as for C++. Your project will be compiled with NativeAOT, meaning it will be able to run on players' machines without needing them to have .NET installed! To build on Windows, that needs Visual Studio or the Build Tools with the Desktop development with C++ workload. For other platforms, you also need the appropriate build tools. See Packaging a build.

title: Console & CVars
text: The console lets you change engine settings and run tasks while the engine is running. Console variables (CVars) CVars are global settings you can change on the fly. Most of them start out with values from Config/EngineConfig.json, and can be changed from the editor's console. Type the name, then the value. Names aren't case sensitive, and you can use the full name or just the last part: ssgi 1 Rendering.SSGI false Bools take true / false (or 1 / 0), numbers and strings work as well As you type, the console suggests CVar and commandlet names. Use Up and Down to pick one, Tab to fill it in, and Esc to dismiss the list. There's no full list yet. To find them all, search the codebase for the regex ^CVar<([A-Za-z_]+)>. Commandlets Commandlets are self-contained tasks, like precompiling shaders, building lighting, baking textures, etc... Even our "Cache server" is a standalone commandlet application. How to run a commandlet: From the console, in editor or in game: type its name, then any arguments. From the command line: pass --exec to an engine executable, followed by the name and arguments, like hyperion-sample.exe --exec MyCommandlet arg1 arg2. As their own program: some special standalone commandlets, like PrecompileShaders, are also built into their own executables. To find every commandlet, search for : public CommandletBase.

title: Scene management
heading: The parts that make up your game
text: A world is your whole game. It holds one or more scenes, which you can think of as levels or regions. Each scene is a tree of nodes. Entities are nodes with components attached, and systems process those components every frame. Scenes can also be assigned to cells on a grid and streamed in and out as the player moves around. The glossary defines each of these terms.

title: Scene management
heading: In this section
text: Entities & components Creating entities, adding components, and moving them. Writing a system Write a custom system in Hyperion Engine World streaming Stream content into the world dynamically Swatches Variations of your world, with different sets for lighting (or other properties)

title: Entities & components
text: Entities are the objects in your scenes. Components hold their data, such as meshes, physics bodies and scripts.

title: Entities & components
heading: Making an entity
text: An entity is a node you can attach components to, so it lives in the scene tree like any other node. Make one, then add it to your scene: Handle<Entity> crate = MakeHandle<Entity>(); crate->SetName(NAME("Crate")); scene->GetRoot()->AddChild(crate); Once it's in a scene, it automatically gets a TransformComponent, a BoundingBoxComponent and a VisibilityStateComponent.

title: Entities & components
heading: Adding components
text: Components are plain structs: MeshComponent meshComponent; meshComponent.mesh = crateMesh; meshComponent.material = crateMaterial; crate->AddComponent<MeshComponent>(meshComponent); crate->SetLocalBounds(crateMesh->GetAABB()); Other component methods: GetComponent<T>() returns a reference. The component must exist! TryGetComponent<T>() returns a pointer, or nullptr if it's missing. HasComponent<T>() checks for one. RemoveComponent<T>() removes it.

title: Entities & components
heading: Transforms
text: Entities are nodes, so they've got a transform. The Local setters are relative to the parent, the World ones aren't: crate->SetLocalTranslation(Vec3f(0.0f, 2.0f, 0.0f)); crate->SetWorldScale(Vec3f(2.0f, 2.0f, 2.0f)); crate->Translate(Vec3f(1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f)); // relative to where it is now To look a node up by name: scene->FindNodeByName("Crate"_sh).

title: Entities & components
heading: Built-in components
text: Common ones: Component What it's for MeshComponent The mesh, material and skeleton to draw. TransformComponent Position, rotation and scale. RigidBodyComponent Makes it a physics body. CharacterControllerComponent Player-style movement: walking, jumping and collision. ScriptComponent Attaches a script. See your first script. AnimationComponent Animation playback. AudioComponent Plays sounds from the entity's position.

title: Entities & components
heading: Making your own
text: Declare a struct with HYP_STRUCT(Component), and mark up the fields you want saved and shown in the editor: HYP_STRUCT(Component, Label = "Health Component") struct HealthComponent { HYP_STRUCT_BODY(HealthComponent); HYP_FIELD(Property = "Health", Serialize, Editor) float health = 100.0f; }; Then include the generated file in your .cpp: #include <HealthComponent.generated.inl> Re-run CodeGen (reconfiguring CMake runs it) to register the component. To process it every frame, write a system.

title: Writing a system
text: The "S" in ECS

title: Writing a system
heading: The basics
text: Subclass SystemBase, list the components you care about, and implement Process. This one regenerates health on anything with a HealthComponent: HYP_CLASS(NoScriptBindings, Serialize = false) class RegenSystem final : public SystemBase { HYP_OBJECT_BODY(RegenSystem); public: void Process(float delta, Span<Handle<Scene>> scenes) override; private: SystemComponentDescriptors GetComponentDescriptors() const override { return { ComponentDescriptor<HealthComponent, ComponentAccess::READ_WRITE> {} }; } }; The implementation: void RegenSystem::Process(float delta, Span<Handle<Scene>> scenes) { if (!GetWorld()->GetGameState().IsSimulating()) { return; } for (Scene* scene : scenes) { for (auto [entity, healthComponent] : scene->GetEntityManager()->GetEntitySet<HealthComponent>().GetScopedView(GetComponentInfos())) { if (healthComponent.health < 100.0f) { healthComponent.health += 5.0f * delta; } } } } The IsSimulating() check skips processing while editing, so it only runs during play.

title: Writing a system
heading: Component access
text: Systems can run in parallel. Saying which components you only READ and which you WRITE lets the engine work out what's safe to run at the same time. Only ask for WRITE access where you need it.

title: Writing a system
heading: Adding it to the world
text: Systems live on the world, not on a scene, and run over every scene in it: GetWorld()->AddSystemT<RegenSystem>();

title: Writing a system
heading: Subsystems
text: For world-wide logic that isn't tied to entities, like a day/night clock or a matchmaking queue, use a subsystem. Subclass Subsystem, fill in OnAddedToWorld(), OnRemovedFromWorld() and Update(float delta), then: GetWorld()->AddSubsystem<MySubsystem>(); A world has at most one of each subsystem type. Retrieve it with GetSubsystem<MySubsystem>().

title: World streaming
text: Stream content into the world dynamically

title: World streaming
heading: How it works
text: Every world has a world grid, made up of one or more layers. Each layer is a grid of streaming cells. Cells within range of a streaming volume are loaded (and cells out of range are unloaded). Cameras have one, and in multiplayer the server keeps one around each connected player.

title: World streaming
heading: Putting a scene on the grid
text: Each scene has a streaming centroid: the grid cell it belongs to. Set it in the scene's properties in the editor, and when the scene is added to the world, it lands on the built-in scenes layer at that spot.

title: World streaming
heading: Layer settings
text: Each layer has these settings: Setting What it does cellSize How big each cell is. Defaults to 32. maxDistance How far out from the volume's cell to load, counted in cells. Defaults to 1. The terrain layer uses 8. infinite Whether the grid goes on forever. Useful for infinite terrain generation. Defaults to on. range The cells the grid covers when it isn't infinite, as a min and max used for both axes. Defaults to -10 to 10.

title: Swatches
text: Variations of your world, with different sets for lighting (or other properties)

title: Swatches
heading: High level overview.
text: Every world starts out with a swatch called Default. Additional swatches can override entity properties, such as the sun angle or light colors. Anything that isn't overridden is shared. Lightmaps and probes are baked per swatch, so each swatch has its own baked lighting rather than relying on realtime lighting when the time of day changes.

title: Swatches
heading: In the editor
text: The active swatch is shown in the toolbar, next to . Add one with New Swatch... in that menu and make it active. With Override Edits on, changes you make are saved as overrides for the active swatch. With it off, they apply to the base as well. The toggle only shows while a swatch other than Default is active. The Inspector's Swatch Overrides section shows what the active swatch overrides on the selected entity, and can reset overrides or copy them from another swatch.

title: Swatches
heading: From code
text: Switch swatches with SetActiveSwatch on the world. It re-applies the swatch's overrides and baked lighting, and the active swatch is saved with the world. world->SetActiveSwatch(NAME("Dusk")); world.SetActiveSwatch(new Name("Dusk")); From the console: setswatch --swatch=Dusk GetSwatchNames() lists them, GetActiveSwatchName() returns the current one, and OnActiveSwatchChanged fires when it changes.

title: Scripting
text: Gameplay scripts can be written in Strata or C# Hyperion supports scripting with C#. Scripts can be attached to individual objects to define behaviour.

title: Scripting
heading: Exposing C++ to scripts
text: Engine types show up in both languages through reflection. Add a class in C++ with reflection macros, and Hyperion's CodeGenTool generates binding code so you can use it in scripts. HYP_CLASS() class Camera : public Entity { HYP_OBJECT_BODY(Camera); public: HYP_METHOD(Property = "FOV") float GetFOV() const; HYP_METHOD(Property = "FOV") void SetFOV(float v); };

title: Scripting
heading: In shipped games
text: When you package a game, C# scripts are compiled ahead of time with NativeAOT, so the game doesn't need .NET installed.

title: Scripting
heading: In this section
text: Your first script Attach a script to an entity and make it move. Calling engine code How engine types show up in Strata and C#, and how to expose your own. Samples Example scripts

title: Your first script
text: Create a script, attach it to an entity, and make the entity move.

title: Your first script
heading: Create a script
text: Select an entity in the Scene panel. In the Inspector, find the Script section, open its More actions menu, and pick Create New Script. Choose the language of the script, and give it a name. Strata is temporarily disabled in current builds, so only C# is offered for now. The editor adds a ScriptComponent to the entity, and saves the file to Content/Scripts/<Name>.strata or Content/Scripts/<Name>.cs in your project. The new script looks like this: using Hyperion; public class NewScript : Script { public override void OnAdded(Entity entity) { } public override void Update(float deltaTime) { } public override void Destroy() { } } import Engine; Entity g_entity; void OnAdded(const Entity entity) { g_entity = entity; } void Update(float delta) { } void Destroy() { } In C#, the class is named after the script.

title: Your first script
heading: Lifecycle
text: Both languages use the same three functions. In Strata they're plain functions in the file; in C# they're overrides on Script. Function When it's called OnAdded When play starts. Receives the entity the script is attached to. Update Every frame while the game is running, with the time since the last frame. Destroy When the entity goes away, or you stop playing. All three are optional. Each entity gets its own copy of the script's state: its own Strata globals, or its own instance of the C# class. Entities sharing a script don't share state.

title: Your first script
heading: Moving the entity
text: This moves the entity upward while the game runs: using Hyperion; public class NewScript : Script { public override void OnAdded(Entity entity) { base.OnAdded(entity); } public override void Update(float deltaTime) { Entity.Translate(new Vec3f(0.0f, deltaTime, 0.0f)); } } import Engine; Entity g_entity; void OnAdded(const Entity entity) { g_entity = entity; } void Update(float delta) { g_entity.Translate(float3(0.0, delta, 0.0)); } In C#, calling base.OnAdded(entity) sets the script's Entity property. The editor's template leaves it out, so add it when you want to use Entity.

title: Your first script
heading: Live reload
text: Saving the file recompiles it in the editor, in either language. While playing, entities using the script get Destroy, the new code is loaded, and OnAdded runs again. Script state is reset on reload. If a script throws, it's marked as errored and stops getting Update calls, until the script runs without throwing.

title: Calling engine code
text: Scripts call into the engine through bindings that CodeGen generates from reflected C++ types, for both Strata and C#.

title: Calling engine code
heading: The engine API
text: Strata is temporarily disabled in current builds, so the Strata examples here aren't applicable yet - the C# ones work as shown In Strata, import Engine; pulls in the generated bindings: handles for engine types, their methods, plus structs and enums. They're written to Data/Scripts/Strata/Engine.strata when you build, which is the quickest way to see what's available. In C#, using Hyperion; brings in the engine's C# classes. Their methods come from extension methods that CodeGen writes to Source/Generated/CSharp/.

title: Calling engine code
heading: Calling methods
text: Methods are called with dot syntax. Methods from parent types work too, so an Entity can do anything a Node can: float3 position = g_entity.GetWorldTranslation(); g_entity.Translate(float3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)); Vec3f position = Entity.GetWorldTranslation(); Entity.Translate(new Vec3f(1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f));

title: Calling engine code
heading: Exposing your own C++
text: Anything reflected is exposed by default. That's HYP_CLASS, HYP_STRUCT and HYP_ENUM types, and HYP_METHOD methods: HYP_CLASS() class Door : public Entity { HYP_OBJECT_BODY(Door); public: HYP_METHOD() void Open(); HYP_METHOD(Property = "Locked") bool IsLocked() const; HYP_METHOD(Property = "Locked") void SetLocked(bool locked); }; The next CodeGen run generates roughly this for each language: handle Door : Entity; impl Door { extern void Open(Door self); extern bool IsLocked(Door self); extern void SetLocked(Door self, bool locked); property bool Locked { get = Door_IsLocked; set = Door_SetLocked; } } public static class DoorExtensions { public static void Open(this Door obj) { ... } public static bool IsLocked(this Door obj) { ... } public static void SetLocked(this Door obj, bool locked) { ... } } In Strata, a getter and setter that share a Property name become a property. In C# they stay as methods. For C#, CodeGen only writes the extension methods. The Door class itself is declared by hand, with a [ClassBinding] attribute naming the C++ class, like the engine's classes in Source/Engine/DotNET/Runtime/: [ClassBinding(Name = "Door")] public class Door : Entity { }

title: Calling engine code
heading: Hiding things from scripts
text: To keep a type or method out of scripts, add NoScriptBindings: HYP_METHOD(NoScriptBindings) void InternalOnly(); To expose a type or method to one language only, use OnlyLanguages with "strata" or "csharp": HYP_METHOD(OnlyLanguages = "csharp") void ForCSharpOnly();

title: Samples
text: To try one of these - create a script in the sample's language (Inspector › Script › Create New Script), paste the sample in, and save it

title: Samples
heading: Health component
text: A custom component that drains over time. C# only (for now). using Hyperion; public struct Health : IComponent { public float Current; public float Max; } public class NewScript : Script { public override void OnAdded(Entity entity) { base.OnAdded(entity); Health health = new Health { Current = 100, Max = 100 }; entity.AddComponent<Health>(ref health); } public override void Update(float deltaTime) { ref Health health = ref Entity.GetComponent<Health>(); health.Current -= deltaTime; Logger.Log(LogLevel.Info, $"Entity health: {health.Current}"); } } Call What it does IComponent Marks the struct as a component type. It's registered when the script loads. AddComponent(ref health) Adds it to the entity GetComponent<Health>() Returns a ref, so changes apply directly Component structs must be blittable: plain value fields, no classes, strings or arrays. By default, a component is saved with the scene and shown in the editor. To change that, add [Component(Flags = ...)] to the struct, with any of ComponentFlags.Serialize, ComponentFlags.ShowInEditor and ComponentFlags.Replicated.

title: Rendering & lighting
heading: Overview
text: Glimmer realtime GI: Hyperion's own global illumination, on by default. Bounce light and sky occlusion are traced in compute shaders, so there's nothing to bake and no ray tracing hardware needed. It runs on desktop and in the browser, and relights instantly when the sun or sky changes. See Glimmer. Backends: DirectX 12 is the default on Windows, and Vulkan is used everywhere else (Linux, Android, and through MoltenVK on Apple platforms). Windows builds can also use Vulkan. Web builds use WebGPU. Clustered deferred shading supports large numbers of dynamic lights. Translucent materials use a forward clustered pass. Baked lighting comes from the lightmapper built into the editor, along with reflection and irradiance probes for moving objects. Glimmer lights everything that isn't lightmapped. Ray tracing: HWRT-supported devices can also use DDGI and ray traced reflections. For non-HWRT we have screen space reflections. Screen space global illumination deprecation is planned so it is not recommended to use Shaders are written in HLSL, compiled with DXC, and reload live in the editor on save.

title: Rendering & lighting
heading: In this section
text: Materials PBR parameters, texture slots and buckets. Lights & shadows Light types and shadow options. Baking lighting Baking lightmaps and probes in the editor. Global illumination The GI options, and how to toggle them. Writing shaders HLSL, permutations and live reload. Post-processing Bloom, TAA, tonemapping, exposure and fog.

title: Materials
text: Materials define how a surface looks: color, roughness, metalness, normals and emission. Hyperion uses a standard PBR model.

title: Materials
heading: Making one
text: In the Assets panel, hit Add... › Material, then open it to edit. It goes in the folder you're browsing. On disk, materials are saved as .hmf files in your project's Content/Materials/ folder.

title: Materials
heading: Parameters
text: Parameter What it does Albedo The base color. White by default. Roughness 0 == perfect mirror, 1 == completely rough surface. As with most things in life, the truth lies somewhere in between. 1 by default. Metalness How metallic the surface is, generally you want 0 or 1 for this. 0 by default. Emissive color, intensity A color and an intensity, for things that glow. NOTE! This is not fully supported in the engine at this point, but lightmap baking will use this to treat a surface as somehting that emits light Alpha threshold Discards pixels for anything with alpha below this value Transmission, IOR For transparent materials like glass. IOR starts at 1.5. UV scale Scales how much the UV coordinates of your mesh repeat: if your textures are stretched across the surface, increase it; too much will cause visible tiling with your textures Unlit Skips lighting entirely Parallax height scale How deep the parallax map goes. 0.02 by default. There are more for foliage and terrain, such as wind, color variation and blending normals with the ground.

title: Materials
heading: Textures
text: The main slots are Diffuse, Normals, Roughness, Metalness, Ambient Occlusion and Parallax. For packed textures (roughness, metalness and AO in one image), you can reuse the same texture in each slot and set which color/alpha channel each one reads for its specific value.

title: Materials
heading: Buckets
text: Each material goes into a bucket, which allows the renderer to decide which pass it is included in as well as other behaviour Opaque: solid surfaces. What you'll want to use, most of the time. Translucent: transparent surfaces, drawn in a separate forward pass. Lightmapped: set automatically when you bake. Sky: Rendered after all others. You likely will not need to use this manually unless you are adding a custom skybox system or something Debug: DebugDrawer stuff - like in editor gizmos, selection boxes, terrain painting cursor, etc.

title: Materials
heading: From code
text: MaterialAttributes attributes; attributes.shaderName = NAME("GeometryPass"); Handle<Material> material = MakeHandle<Material>(NAME("CrateMaterial"), attributes); material->SetTexture(MaterialTextureKey::Diffuse, crateTexture); InitObject(material);

title: Lights & shadows
text: Directional, point, spot and area lights, and how their shadows are rendered.

title: Lights & shadows
heading: Adding a light
text: Use Add › Lighting in the toolbar: Light What it's for Directional Light Light from far away, like the sun. Every new project has one. Point Light Light from a point, in every direction. Spot Light Light from a point, in a cone. Rectangular Area Light Light from a rectangle, like a window or a panel.

title: Lights & shadows
heading: Shadows
text: Each light has flags in the Inspector: Flag What it does Render shadows The light casts shadows. On by default. Cache shadow maps for static objects Static objects' shadows are rendered once and reused, so only moving objects are redrawn each frame. On by default. Only render shadows for static objects Moving objects don't cast shadows from this light. Bake static shadow map Bakes static objects' shadows ahead of time. Only for static point and spot lights.

title: Lights & shadows
heading: Baked static shadows
text: Enabling Bake static shadow map bakes the light's shadow map in the editor. To rebake every light that has this flag, use Bake › Static Shadows.

title: Baking lighting
text: Baking computes lighting ahead of time, so it doesn't have to be calculated while the game runs. It's the main way to get good lighting on lower-end hardware.

title: Baking lighting
heading: How to bake
text: Add a Lightmap Volume around the area you want baked: Add › Lighting › Lightmap Volume. For lighting and reflections on moving objects, add Reflection Probes and Irradiance Probes from the same menu. Click Bake in the toolbar and pick what to bake: Lightmaps, Reflection Probes, Irradiance Probes, Fog Volumes or Static Shadows. Progress is shown in an overlay while the bake runs. When you change something a bake depends on, like moving a static object or a light, the editor shows what needs a rebake in an overlay.

title: Baking lighting
heading: What gets baked
text: Type What it is Lightmaps Light bouncing around your static geometry, saved into textures. Lightmap UVs are generated for you. Reflection probes What the world looks like from a point, for shiny surfaces. Irradiance probes How much light reaches a point, for lighting things that move. Fog volumes Light from static lights scattering through fog volumes. Static shadows Shadow maps for static point and spot lights with Bake static shadow map ticked. See lights & shadows. Baking runs on the GPU. It uses hardware ray tracing when available, and compute shaders otherwise.

title: Baking lighting
heading: Settings
text: Bake settings live in the "Baker" section of Config/EngineConfig.json: Setting What it does NumSamples More samples, less noise, longer bakes. The default config uses 1. MaxRayDistance How far rays travel looking for light. Defaults to 1000. ForceComputeTracing Use the compute path even when hardware ray tracing is available. Also the Baking.ForceComputeTracing CVar. Each swatch has its own bake.

title: Global illumination
text: Global illumination is indirect light: light that bounces off surfaces. Hyperion supports several techniques, from fully baked to realtime, with or without ray tracing hardware.

title: Global illumination
heading: Options
text: What What it does Needs HWRT? Lightmaps Baked bounce light for static geometry. See baking. Glimmer Realtime bounce light and sky occlusion, traced in software. On by default, off on mobile. SSR Reflections from what's on screen. GTAO Soft shadows in corners and crevices. DDGI Realtime bounce light from ray-traced probes. ✓ RT reflections Ray-traced reflections, including things that are off screen. ✓ These can be combined. A typical setup is baked lightmaps and probes, with SSR and GTAO on top.

title: Global illumination
heading: Glimmer
text: Glimmer is Hyperion's realtime GI system. It traces rays in compute shaders rather than requiring ray tracing hardware. Nothing needs baking, so you can rotate the sun, move a local light, or a wall and the bounce light follows. Glimmer supports light bounced/emitted from static geometry and emitted from local lights. Dynamic objects receive its light, but don't affect it. Time of day changes are supported due to Glimmer storing precomputed radiance transfer (PRT) data. Near the camera, probes trace against the scene's meshes. They're placed around solid geometry, so light doesn't leak through walls. Further out, a coarser grid traces a voxelized version of the scene, plus a heightfield for terrain. Changing the sun or sky relights the scene without tracing it again. Static point and spot lights add their bounce light. Lightmapped surfaces keep their lightmaps. Glimmer lights everything else. Sky reflections are dimmed where the sky is blocked, so interiors don't glow with sky color. It's meant for large outdoor worlds, where baking isn't practical. Turn it off per world with Glimmer GI in World Settings, or scale it with Rendering.Glimmer.Intensity. On lower-end devices and on the web, the near-field probes are turned off and only the coarser grid is used. See device tiers.

title: Global illumination
heading: Toggles
text: Each has a console variable. Toggle them from the console; Config/EngineConfig.json and the device tiers can change their defaults: CVar Controls Rendering.LightmapVolumes Baked lightmaps Rendering.Glimmer.Enabled Glimmer Rendering.SSR SSR. Off in the default config. Rendering.GTAO GTAO Rendering.DDGI DDGI. Off by default. Rendering.RayTracing.RayTracedReflections RT reflections. Off by default. Glimmer, DDGI and ray-traced reflections are also set per world, under World Settings in the gear menu. Glimmer and ray-traced reflections start on there; DDGI starts off.

title: Writing shaders
text: Shaders are written in HLSL and compiled with DXC for every backend. The editor reloads them automatically when they change.

title: Writing shaders
heading: Adding a shader
text: Shaders live in Source/Shaders/. Write your .hlsl file, then add it to the Definitions list in Config/Shaders.hmf: ShaderDefinitions "ShaderDefinitions" { Definitions = [ ... ShaderDefinition "MyEffect" { VS = "MyEffect/MyEffect.hlsl" PS = "MyEffect/MyEffect.hlsl" } ] } Paths are relative to Source/Shaders/. The keys are the stages: Key Stage VS Vertex shader PS Pixel shader CS Compute shader RGS, CHS, MS Ray tracing: ray generation, closest hit, and miss Condition = "Rendering.FogVolumes" (any bool CVar) only compiles and uses the shader while that CVar is on.

title: Writing shaders
heading: Permutations
text: Shader variants are declared at the top of the file: PERMUTE(GTAO_ENABLED) PERMUTE(LIGHT_TYPE, CLUSTERED, DIRECTIONAL, POINT, SPOT, AREA_RECT); With just a name, it's an on/off variant. With a list of values, each variant defines one of them, such as LIGHT_TYPE_POINT: #ifdef LIGHT_TYPE_DIRECTIONAL // directional light only #endif STATIC(NAME, value) sets a fixed define.

title: Writing shaders
heading: Precompiling
text: Shipping builds use precompiled shaders. Packaging does this automatically. To run it yourself: PrecompileShaders.exe --platform=windows Add --api=vulkan, --api=dx12 or --api=webgpu to pick a backend, or --filter=MyEffect to limit it to matching shaders. --platform takes windows, mac, linux, android, ios or web.

title: Post-processing
text: Effects applied to the scene

title: Post-processing
heading: Effects
text: Effect Notes Bloom Glow around bright areas. Tuned with Rendering.BloomThreshold and Rendering.BloomIntensity. TAA Smooths out jagged edges over a few frames. Runs on the HDR image, before bloom and tonemapping. Tonemapping AgX, AgX Punchy (the default), ACES, PBR Neutral or Reinhard. Exposure and color Exposure compensation, white balance, tint, saturation, contrast and vignette. Fog and clouds Height fog, fog volumes and clouds.

title: Post-processing
heading: Per-world settings
text: Tonemapping, exposure, color, fog and clouds are per-world settings, under World Settings in the gear menu, along with the sky, sky light and wind.

title: Post-processing
heading: Toggles
text: The heavier effects can be toggled with console variables or config file changes. CVar Controls Rendering.Bloom Bloom Rendering.TAA TAA Rendering.FogVolumes Fog volumes Rendering.Clouds Clouds On mobile, bloom, clouds and fog volumes are off by default. See device tiers.

title: Physics
text: Hyperion uses Jolt Physics for rigid bodies and character controllers

title: Physics
heading: In this section
text: Rigid bodies Rigid bodies, physics materials and collision shapes. Character controllers Walking, running and jumping.

title: Physics
heading: TODO
text: Forces and impulses Physics raycasts Triggers

title: Rigid bodies
text: Rigid bodies allow physics simulation to be applied to your Entities

title: Rigid bodies
heading: In editor:
text: Add aRigidBodyComponent in the editor by seleting the entity in the scene hierarchy, clicking 'Add' > 'Rigid Body Component' under the 'Components' header.

title: Rigid bodies
heading: In code (C++):
text: PhysicsMaterial material; material.mass = 10.0f; crate->AddComponent<RigidBodyComponent>(RigidBodyComponent { .physicsMaterial = material }); Mass defaults to 0, which makes the body static: other bodies collide with it, but it doesn't move. Set a mass above 0 to make it dynamic.

title: Rigid bodies
heading: Physics material
text: Property What it does mass Mass of the body, 0 == static, immovable friction Surface friction. Starts at 0.5. restitution Bounciness. Starts at 0. To give a body a starting velocity, set initialVelocity or initialAngularVelocity on the component

title: Rigid bodies
heading: Shapes
text: The shape defines the collision volume. Make one with Assets › Add... › Physics Shape, and assign it to the component's collision shape. You can pick from: Box, Sphere, Capsule and Plane. Convex hull, wrapped around a mesh. Compound, a mesh decomposed into convex pieces. Use this for complex geometry. Height field, for terrain. Plane and height field bodies are always static, whatever their mass. If no shape is set, a box fitted to the entity's bounds is used.

title: Rigid bodies
heading: In multiplayer
text: The server is the authority, and simulates physics for the world. On clients, replicated bodies don't simulate: they follow the positions and velocities the server sends, interpolating between updates. Bodies that aren't replicated are simulated locally on each client. More in replication.

title: Character controllers
text: The character controller handles walking, running and jumping, with collision against the world.

title: Character controllers
heading: Adding one
text: Add a CharacterControllerComponent to an entity. By default it's driven by keyboard input: Action Key Move W A S D Sprint Shift Jump Space isOnGround is true while it's standing on something, including slopes too steep to walk up.

title: Character controllers
heading: Movement settings
text: These are under movement: Setting What it does moveSpeed Walking speed, in m/s. Starts at 15. sprintSpeed Running speed. Starts at 25. groundAcceleration, airAcceleration How quickly it gets up to speed on the ground, and how much it can steer in the air. friction How quickly it slows down when you let go. stepHeight The tallest step it can walk straight up. Starts at 0.35. maxSlopeAngle The steepest slope it can walk up, in degrees. Starts at 55. orientToMovement Turns the character to face the way it's moving, at turnRate degrees per second. On slopes steeper than maxSlopeAngle, the character slides down, and can still jump off, pushed away from the slope.

title: Character controllers
heading: Jump settings
text: These are under jump: Setting What it does speed Initial jump speed. Starts at 4.9. coyoteTime Grace period for jumping after leaving a ledge. Starts at 0.15 seconds. bufferTime How early before landing a jump press still counts. Starts at 0.15 seconds. cutGravityMultiplier Extra gravity while rising if you let go of jump early, for variable jump height. apexGravityMultiplier, fallGravityMultiplier Gravity near the top of the jump (below 1 gives a little hang time), and while falling.

title: Character controllers
heading: Pushing things
text: Under push, massLimit is the heaviest dynamic body the character can push (350 to start), and maxSpeed caps how fast it pushes it.

title: Character controllers
heading: In multiplayer
text: The local player's movement is predicted on the client, so input responds immediately. The server validates each move and corrects the client if they disagree. More in replication.

title: Plugins
text: Plugins add optional features to the engine and your game. They can extend the editor as well, to provide new tools and workflows.

title: Plugins
heading: Turning plugins on and off
text: Open Plugins... from the editor's settings menu. Each plugin is listed with its version, description and the plugins it depends on. Tick the ones you want. When a plugin is off: its systems, import steps and editor tools don't load, and its C# assemblies aren't used. anything it added to your project's data is kept to prevent losing your data. If you choose to re-enable the plugin, your data will be available again.

title: Plugins
heading: Built-in plugins
text: AnimToolkit Skeletal animation, graphs and the animation editor. Creating your own plugin Layout, modules, and what a plugin can register.

title: AnimToolkit
text: Everything for animated characters: playing clips, blending them with graphs, and editing them in the editor. This doc is a work in progress. AnimToolkit includes two modules. Animation, which your game uses at runtime, and AnimationEditor, which only the editor loads, for in-editor tooling. Without the plugin, skinned meshes still import and draw in their bind pose, and clips still import as assets. They just don't play.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Playing a clip
text: Add an AnimationComponent to an entity with a skinned mesh. Pick a clip under Animation, and tick PlayOnStart to have it play when the game starts. Setting What it does Animation The clip to play. The list only shows clips that fit the entity's skeleton. PlayOnStart Start playing when the game starts. LoopMode Whether the clip plays once or loops. Speed Playback speed. 1 is normal. Graph An animation graph to run instead of a single clip. See below. Importing a model with animations adds the AnimationComponent for you, set to the first clip. You can turn that off in the import settings with AddAnimationComponent. If a clip was made for a different skeleton, or there's no skeleton at all, the Inspector shows a warning.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Animation graphs
text: An animation graph decides which pose a character shows. Instead of switching clips by hand, you build a graph once, then drive it with a few parameters like Speed or Jump from your game. Create one from Assets › Add... › Animation Graph. Double-click a graph in Assets to open it.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Nodes
text: A graph is a set of nodes that each produce a pose. Wire them together and mark one as the output. Node What it does Clip Plays a clip, with a play rate, looping and a start offset. Blend1D Blends clips placed along one parameter, like idle, walk and run on speed. Blend2D Blends clips over two parameters, like forward and sideways velocity. Layer Plays one pose over another, only on the bones in a bone mask. Additive Adds a pose on top of a base pose. ChainTwist Twists a chain of bones, for aiming. Slot A place for gameplay to play a one-off clip, like an emote, over the graph. FootIK Plants the feet on the ground. StateMachine Moves between states, each with its own pose. Clips in a sync group share their phase, so blended walk and run cycles keep their feet in step.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: State machines
text: Double-click a StateMachine node to open it. States are boxes and transitions are arrows. Right-click a state and pick Make Transition, then click the state it leads to. Each transition has a duration, a blend curve, a priority, and conditions that read like sentences: Speed > 0.5, Jump is triggered, time in state >= 0.3s.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Parameters
text: The Parameters panel lists the values your game sets. They can be floats, bools, triggers or vectors. While you're editing, drag a value and watch the preview character blend.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Character models
text: CharacterModelComponent drives a character from its character controller. It works out speed, direction, whether it's in the air and so on, and feeds them to the graph. It also handles which way the character faces, turn-in-place steps and aiming. By default it runs the built-in HumanoidMotionMatching graph, so a humanoid character animates with no setup. To use your own, set Graph. Setting What it does Graph The animation graph to run. FacingMode, TurnSharpness Which way the body faces, and how quickly it turns to it. AlignToCapsule, ModelOffset Where the model sits inside the character controller's capsule. FootIK Plants the feet on uneven ground. FootProbeHeight, FootProbeDepth and FootIKSmoothing tune it. ApplyRootMotion Moves the character with the motion baked into the clip.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Humanoids and retargeting
text: A skeleton can be marked as a humanoid by mapping its bones to standard slots like hips, spine and the arm and leg chains. The editor can map common rigs for you. Once two skeletons are mapped, a clip made for one plays on the other. Rotations carry over bone by bone, and the hips movement is scaled to fit the new character's height.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Bone attachments
text: Put a BoneAttachmentComponent on an entity to make it follow a bone or socket of another character, like a sword in a hand. Sockets are named points on a skeleton, with an offset from their bone.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Editing animation
text: Right-click an animated entity and pick Edit Animation, or double-click a skeleton or clip in Assets. The editor opens a preview of the character: the hierarchy shows its bones, and you can add sockets to them; a timeline bar under the viewport plays the clip and lets you scrub and add markers; Show Bones in the tools menu draws the skeleton in the viewport. Make your changes, then Apply to save them or Revert to throw them away.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Editing a graph
text: Right-click an entity and pick Edit Animation Graph, or double-click a graph in Assets. The graph opens in the bottom dock beside Assets and Console, with the viewport and preview character above it. Press Space on the canvas to search for a node to add. Select a node to edit its settings in the main Inspector. Press Home to frame the whole graph. Graphs that come with the engine are read-only. Use Copy to Project to get an editable copy that's assigned to your character.

title: AnimToolkit
heading: Debugging while playing
text: On a CharacterModelComponent or AnimationComponent, Open Graph attaches the graph to the running character. The current state, running transitions and node weights light up as you play, and the Parameters panel shows live values. Picking which character to debug Opening a new graph as soon as it's created

title: Creating your own plugin
text: Writing a plugin for Hyperion Engine. Plugins are built with the engine for now, so you can develop yours inside of the engine's Source/Plugins folder alongside other built-in plugins.

title: Creating your own plugin
heading: Layout
text: Make a folder in Source/Plugins named after your plugin: MyPlugin/ MyPlugin.hypplugin Source/ MyPlugin/ runtime module MyPluginEditor/ editor module (optional) Managed/ C# (optional) Content/ assets (optional) Tests/ Every folder under Source is a module, and the engine's build finds each of them. Ensure you run the build script (build.bat / build.sh) and press Y to reconfigure CMake after adding one, as well as when you add or remove a file/folder in here. A module whose name ends in Editor is only built into the editor. A module built for the editor may use the runtime modules, but a runtime module cannot use an editor module!

title: Creating your own plugin
heading: The descriptor
text: MyPlugin.hypplugin is an HMF file: PluginDescriptor "MyPlugin" { Version = "1.0.0" Description = "A plugin that does something." EnabledByDefault = false } Setting What it does Version Shown in the Plugins window. Description Shown in the Plugins window. EnabledByDefault Whether new projects have it on. Dependencies Names of plugins this one needs, they will come along for the ride. EngineMinVersion The oldest engine version it works with.

title: Creating your own plugin
heading: A module
text: Each module is a class that implements IPluginModule, plus one macro to register it. OnLoad runs when the plugin is enabled, and gets a PluginContext to register things through: #include <Plugins/PluginModule.hpp> #include <Plugins/PluginContext.hpp> namespace Hyperion { class MyPluginModule final : public IPluginModule { public: void OnLoad(PluginContext& context) override { context.RegisterWorldSystem<MySystem>(); } }; } // namespace Hyperion HYP_DEFINE_PLUGIN_MODULE(MyPlugin, MyPlugin, ::Hyperion::MyPluginModule) The HYP_DEFINE_PLUGIN_MODULE macro takes the plugin's name, the module's name (the folder name) and the class. Anything you register through the context is removed again when the plugin unloads.

title: Creating your own plugin
heading: What a plugin can register
text: Call What it does RegisterWorldSystem<T>() Adds a system to every world. Optionally limit it to worlds with certain flags, or by a predicate. RegisterModelImportProcessor<T>() Runs after a model is imported, to add components or tweak the result. It can have its own import settings. AddCleanup(fn) Runs when the plugin unloads, for anything you set up yourself. Components and other reflected classes (HYP_CLASS, HYP_STRUCT) register themselves, like they do in a game. Files in Content are added to the engine's assets. If you need to know where you're running, IsEditorHost() and GetHostMode() on the context tell you.

title: Creating your own plugin
heading: Editor modules
text: In an Editor module, RegisterEditorExtension<T>(context) adds an EditorExtension. It gets Update, DebugDraw and picking hooks for the viewport. There are similar calls for dropping assets onto entities and for setting up a new player.

title: Creating your own plugin
heading: Editor UI in C#
text: Editor panels and menus are written in C# with Avalonia, in the plugin's Managed folder. Mark a class with [EditorPlugin] and implement IEditorPlugin: [EditorPlugin("MyPlugin")] public sealed class MyPluginEditor : IEditorPlugin { public void Register(EditorPluginRegistry registry) { registry.RegisterView<MyPanelViewModel, MyPanelView>(); registry.AddToolMenuItem("My Panel...", new RelayCommand( () => PanelService.Instance.OpenPanel(new MyPanelViewModel()))); } } The registry also lets you add: Call What it does AddNodeMenuItem An entry in the Scene panel's right-click menu. AddDocument A document that docks in the editor, like AnimToolkit's graph editor. AddEditModeBar A bar that shows in a custom edit mode. RegisterPropertyEditor A custom Inspector control for fields marked with EditorType = "...". AddComponentInspectorItem An extra row under a component in the Inspector. AddInspectorWarning A warning the Inspector shows for an entity. AddCreatableAssetClass, RegisterAssetIcon Make an asset type creatable from Add... and give it an icon. AddEntityDropAssetClass Let an asset type be dropped onto entities.

title: Creating your own plugin
heading: Examples
text: AnimToolkit in Source/Plugins/AnimToolkit is the full-size one. For something small to copy, Tests/Plugins/PluginTest has a system, an import processor, an editor extension, a panel and some content, in about a dozen files.

title: Running a server
heading: Start a server
text: The game executable runs as a server with --server: hyperion-sample --server --gameport=9192 It runs headless (no window), and reads console commands from its terminal. Leave off --gameport and it uses the Net.GameServerPort CVar, which defaults to 9192. A headless server ticks at up to 60 times a second, set with Sim.HeadlessTickRate. Add --startupworld=<WorldName> to pick the world it starts in.

title: Running a server
heading: Connect a client
text: Run the game executable with --host to connect to the server at that address: hyperion-sample --host=127.0.0.1 --gameport=9192 With --autoconnect=false, or without --host, it shows a screen where you can change the address before connecting, or pick Single Player instead.

title: Running a server
heading: Your own game
text: A game built from the editor takes the same flags. It starts in single player by default, because its Config/GlobalConfig.json passes --singleplayer. Pass --singleplayer=false to override it. For example: MyGame --server # start standalone a server MyGame --singleplayer=false --host=127.0.0.1 # connect to a server

title: Running a server
heading: From the editor
text: The editor can start a local server and connect to it for play-in-editor with networking. See play-in-editor for info

title: Replication & prediction
text: The server runs the authoritative game state and sends updates to clients, which interpolate and predict between them.

title: Replication & prediction
heading: Replicating an entity
text: Add the Replicated tag on the server: entity->AddTag<EntityTag::Replicated>(); The server assigns it a network ID and sends its transform (plus velocities, for physics bodies) to clients. Clients only receive updates for entities within 50 units of them.

title: Replication & prediction
heading: Interpolation
text: Updates don't arrive every frame, so clients render slightly behind and interpolate between the last couple of updates. When updates are late, dead reckoning guesses where things are headed. CVar What it does Net.InterpolationEnabled Turns interpolation on or off. Net.InterpolationDelay How far behind to stay, in seconds. Starts at 0.1. Net.DeadReckoning Turns dead reckoning on or off. Net.InterpRatio Stays at least this many update intervals behind, if that's more than Net.InterpolationDelay. Starts at 2.

title: Replication & prediction
heading: Client-side prediction
text: The local player's movement is predicted: The client applies the move immediately and sends it to the server. The server replays the move and acknowledges the resulting position. The client compares that with its prediction and corrects any difference. When they disagree, the client rewinds to the server's position, replays the moves the server hasn't acknowledged yet, and smooths out the difference over at least Net.CorrectionSmoothingTime (0.1 seconds to start). If they're more than Net.CorrectionThreshold apart (4 units to start), it's treated as a teleport and snaps straight there.

title: Replication & prediction
heading: Authority
text: The server has authority. So does a game that isn't connected to anything, like single player. On clients, replicated physics bodies are driven by server updates.

title: Replication & prediction
heading: Not yet supported
text: There are no RPCs yet, and you can't replicate individual properties or components. Replication currently covers which entities exist (their class, name, parent and scene) and their transforms.
