text: Platform Status Windows (x64, arm64) Yes. Runtime and editor. DirectX 12 by default, or Vulkan. macOS (arm64) Yes. Runtime and editor. Linux (x64) Yes. Runtime and editor. Web Yes, through WebAssembly and WebGPU. Runtime only, built from the Windows editor. Android Supported - not stable yet. iOS Supported - not stable yet. Steam Deck Yes, through Proton. Input and resolution handling still need work. Linux is newer than the other desktop platforms, so expect some rough edges. Contributions are welcome on this front (as well as anywhere else).

title: Platforms
heading: In this section
text: Packaging a build Build a standalone copy of your game to distribute. Web Build your game for the browser. Android Building and installing on Android devices. iOS Build for iPhone and iPad through Xcode.

title: Platforms
heading: Steam Deck
text: On the Deck, run the Windows build through Proton. Controller input and resolution handling still need work here. The native Linux build hasn't been tested on the Deck yet.

title: Platforms
heading: Per-platform settings
text: Each platform can have its own config, like Config/EngineConfig.Android.json or Config/GlobalConfig.Web.json. If a platform file exists it replaces the regular one, rather than merging with it, so it needs every setting. The mobile configs, for example, turn off ray tracing, DDGI, SSGI and TAA.

title: Platforms
heading: Device tiers
text: On top of the config, Config/DeviceTiers.hmf has rules that change settings for the device the game is running on. Each rule matches on any of: Axis Values DeviceType Desktop, Laptop, Mobile DevicePlatform Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android, IOS, Web DeviceGrade Low, Medium, High, Ultra and overrides the EngineConfig settings it lists. When matches exact values, and AtMost matches a grade or anything below it: TierRule "Web" { When = { DevicePlatform = Web } Set = { "Rendering.Glimmer.Probes.Enabled" = false } } The Mobile rule, for example, turns off Glimmer, SSR, clouds, fog volumes, shadows and bloom. To test another tier, force an axis from the command line with --devicetype, --deviceplatform or --devicegrade, like --devicegrade=Low.

title: Packaging a build
text: Packaging turns your project into a standalone build you can distribute. The examples on this page describe how to package your game and run it on Windows, but other platforms are nearly the same. For macOS/Linux, use the bash scripts where batch scripts would be used. For example, build.bat becomes build.sh. For executables, (MyGame.exe), use MyGame (no extension).

title: Packaging a build
heading: What packaging does
text: Cooks your project's content, and the engine's, into a compact cache. Includes compiled shaders, so the game doesn't need shader source. Copies the executable, content and config into one folder that runs by itself. There are two ways to do it: from the editor, or with the packaging scripts in the engine repo.

title: Packaging a build
heading: From the editor
text: This packages the game you built with Build Game, so do that first. Choose Build › Package Game... in the toolbar. Pick a folder to put the package in. The editor saves your project and will begin packaging your game. When it's done, your file browser will open at the output directory. Example structure: MyGame/ Packaged/Build_20261022_153000/ MyGame.exe MyGameGame.dll hyperion.dll Cache/ Content/ Config/ Run MyGame.exe to start your game. Folder What's in it Cache Cooked asset data and compiled shaders Content Asset manifests, for your project and for the engine (Content/Engine) Config Engine settings, and the game's launch arguments in GlobalConfig.json The game starts in the world you had open when you packaged it, in single player. Both are set in Config/GlobalConfig.json. A C# game is compiled ahead of time with NativeAOT, so the package runs on a machine without .NET installed. To package this, you need the .NET 10 SDK, and on Windows, Visual Studio or the Build Tools with the Desktop development with C++ workload. Packaging from the editor builds for the platform the editor is running on. For the browser, use Build › Package for Web. See Web.

title: Packaging a build
heading: Packaging settings
text: Build › Packaging Settings... has settings for the cook, saved with your project: Setting What it does Max Texture Size The largest texture dimension in the cooked game. Bigger textures are scaled down. 0 means no limit. Defaults apply everywhere. Use Platform Override to change a setting for one platform; anything you don't override follows the defaults. New projects start with overrides for the web (256), iOS (512) and Android (512).

title: Packaging a build
heading: Multiplayer
text: The packaged game hosts and joins games with the same flags as the built one: MyGame --server # start a standalone server MyGame --singleplayer=false --host=127.0.0.1 # connect to a server

title: Packaging a build
heading: With the packaging scripts
text: The scripts in the engine repo make a shipping build (optimized, no editor, no debug checks) and package the sample game with your project's content. Build Release first. Packaging uses the shader and cooking tools from the Release build. build.bat Release Run the packaging script from the root of the repo. It makes its own shipping build, with Clang and Ninja, so you'll need both: Tools\Scripts\PackageBuildWindows.bat When it asks, type your project's folder name (the one under Projects/). Your build lands in PackagedBuilds/Windows/Build_<date>_<time>/. The game executable is hyperion-sample.exe. The Windows package includes Steam's test app files (app ID 480) so Steam features work while you're developing. Swap in your own app ID before you ship.

title: Packaging a build
heading: Other platforms
text: There are matching scripts for macOS (PackageBuildMacOS.sh), iOS (PackageBuildIOS.sh), Android (PackageBuildAndroid.bat) and the web (PackageBuildWeb.bat) in Tools/Scripts/. Android, iOS and the web have their own pages: Android, iOS and Web. The macOS and iOS scripts are still a work in progress.

title: Packaging a build
heading: About shipping builds
text: To make a shipping build without packaging it: build.bat Shipping It goes into Binaries/<Platform>/Shipping/, without the editor, tests or commandlets.

title: Web
text: Hyperion games can run in the browser, built to WebAssembly and rendered with WebGPU.

title: Web
heading: What you'll need
text: Web builds are made on Windows (for now), from an editor you built from source. emsdk, with EMSDK pointing at it. The engine's web build is made with Emscripten 6.0.11. Ninja on your PATH. PowerShell 7 (pwsh), for compressing the cooked content. Python on your PATH, to serve the build locally. The engine built for the web, plus a regular Windows Release build (packaging uses its cooking tools): build.bat Web Release build.bat Release The web build checks that the engine's web libraries are newer than its source, and asks you to rebuild them if not.

title: Web
heading: From the editor
text: Item What it does Build › Package for Web Cooks your content and builds the game into Binaries/Web in your project folder. Play in Web Browser (in the menu next to Play) Builds if needed, then serves the build locally and opens it in your browser. The editor can't build C# game projects for the web yet. Binaries/Web is a plain folder of static files, so any static host can serve it as it is. Intermediate files go to Build/Web. New projects limit textures to 256 pixels for the web, to keep downloads small. Change it in Packaging Settings.

title: Web
heading: With the script
text: Tools/Scripts/BuildWebGame.ps1 does the same as the editor: pwsh Tools/Scripts/BuildWebGame.ps1 -Project Projects/MyGame -Run Option What it does -Run Serves the build afterwards and opens it in your browser. -ServeOnly Skips the build, and serves the last one. -FastLink Links at -O1 instead of -Oz: minutes faster, for testing locally. -MaxTextureSize Overrides the texture limit. -Worlds The worlds to include, comma separated. Defaults to the world being edited. To serve a build you've already made: Tools\Scripts\ServeWeb.bat Projects\MyGame (port 8080 unless you pass another).

title: Web
heading: Sample
text: You can play a web build of our sample game right now.

title: Android
text: Hyperion runs on Android phones and tablets. Support works, but isn't stable yet.

title: Android
heading: What you'll need
text: The Android NDK. We test with NDK 29. Point ANDROID_NDK_HOME at it. Ninja, on your PATH or installed with Visual Studio or the Android SDK. The Android SDK and Java 17, for Gradle. Android Studio installs both. A regular Windows Release build of the engine (build.bat Release). Packaging uses its shader and cooking tools. We build for 64-bit ARM (arm64-v8a), and you'll need Android 9 (API 28) or newer.

title: Android
heading: Build it
text: Build the engine for Android and package it with your project's content: Tools\Scripts\PackageBuildAndroid.bat --cook --project MyGame This makes its own shipping build for Android, so you don't need to run build.bat Android first. --project is the project's folder name under Projects/. Without --cook, only engine content is included. --skip-precompile skips precompiling shaders. The package lands in PackagedBuilds/Android/Build_<date>_<time>/. Build and install the APK with Gradle, from Source/PlatformSpecific/Android/: gradlew.bat installDebug Gradle picks up the last package automatically. You can also open that folder in Android Studio and run it from there. To build only the engine libraries, without packaging: build.bat Android Release. They end up in Binaries/Android/Release/.

title: Android
heading: Settings
text: Android uses Config/EngineConfig.Android.json instead of the regular config with platform-specific overrides for targeting lower end devices than the typical desktop experience. The Mobile device tier rule applies on top of it.

title: iOS
text: Hyperion runs on iPhone and iPad through MoltenVK. Like Android, support isn't stable yet.

title: iOS
heading: What you'll need
text: A Mac with Xcode. The Vulkan SDK, with VULKAN_SDK set. It comes with MoltenVK, which we link for iOS. A device on iOS 14 or newer.

title: iOS
heading: Build it
text: From the root of the repo, generate an Xcode project: ./Tools/Scripts/BuildHyperion.sh IOS Xcode Release regenerate Open it in Xcode, pick your team under Signing (we leave signing off by default), and run it on your device.

title: iOS
heading: Packaging
text: Tools/Scripts/PackageBuildIOS.sh makes a shipping build for iOS and packages it with your project's content. It needs a Mac Release build first, for the shader and cooking tools, and asks for your project's folder name under Projects/. The package lands in PackagedBuilds/IOS/Build_<date>_<time>/. The script is still a work in progress.

title: iOS
heading: Notes
text: There's no editor on iOS. iOS uses Config/EngineConfig.IOS.json, which turns off the same rendering features as Android, plus SSR, and targets 30 FPS. The Mobile device tier rule applies on top of it.
